newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-U.S. MEET DIRECTOR TO ACCEPT SLANEY ENTRY.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-U.S. MEET DIRECTOR TO ACCEPT SLANEY ENTRY.

text.p: U.S. officials will accept suspended runner Mary Slaney's entry into this week's national championships, the meet's director said on Monday. But the American federation would not say whether it would defy the IAAF's suspension of the U.S. star and permit her to run in the world championships qualifier that begins on Wednesday.
"I have an entry, it is in on time and I have not received any instructions that it not be accepted," meeting director Duffy Mahoney, the U.S. federation's director of operations, told Reuters.

Mahoney declined to elaborate, and U.S. spokesman Pete Cava said he was unable to say what would happen. But another U.S. official, who asked not to be named, said Slaney would be permitted to run only if she obtained a court order.
The Americans are still waiting for official notification of the suspensions from the IAAF before taking action.

Slaney, holder of numerous U.S. distance records, and two other U.S. athletes were suspended by the IAAF last week pending the outcome of U.S. hearings into alleged doping cases. Until the cases are resolved, the three will not be allowed to compete, even in the U.S. championships, an IAAF spokesman said.

Slaney, who was found to have a higher than acceptable ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone in a doping test at last June's U.S. Olympic trials, has consistently denied taking steroids or any substance banned by the IAAF.
Her husband, former British discus thrower Richard Slaney, expressed outrage that the case had not been resolved.
"If we went to court, why would we ask for a restraining order," Slaney said from his home in Eugene, Oregon. "She doesn't have a positive test and she has not been suspended by the U.S. federation."
He said Slaney had not decided whether to compete in the championships.
"It's her decision, but if it were mine, I would not fly all the way back there to have some jerk say she cannot run," Richard Slaney said.
